rubrics.title: What Is a Scientist? AI Creation Assignment

ratings.long_description: Image is creative, detailed, and clearly represents what a scientist is or does.
Reflection connects thoughtfully to the image and shows original insight. Names the independent, dependent, and controlled variables.
Submission is complete, labeled correctly, and follows all directions with care.

rubrics.title: Rube Goldberg: The Endless Energy Machine

ratings.long_description: Includes 5+ steps showing realistic energy transfer and motion. Clearly follows the Law of Conservation of Energy.
Uses models, colliders, and chain reactions in a unique and well-planned way.
Clear 2D video demonstrates the system in motion. Shows understanding of energy movement.
Scene is neat, complete, and presented with enthusiasm and scientific purpose.

rubrics.title: Science Notebook Assignment: Potential vs. Kinetic Energy

criteria.description: Two labeled drawings for Potential Energy
Two labeled drawings for Kinetic Energy

rubrics.title: Forces Unleashed: The Science Comic Challenge

ratings.long_description: Demonstrates a clear understanding of applied force, gravity, and friction; shows how each affects motion accurately.
Engaging and original story with one chosen villain; shows problem-solving and teamwork between forces.
Visually appealing comic layout that fits on one page; uses AI tools effectively; strong attention to detail and effort.

rubrics.title: Science Notebook Entry: Field Scientist Challenge

ratings.long_description: Three or more clear, evidence-based observations written in notebook.
Two or more logical inferences supported by observations.
One complete and reasonable hypothesis using correct format.
CLEAR photo uploaded to Canvas.

rubrics.title: The Science Trainer Challenge: Mastering the Method

ratings.long_description: Each of the six steps of the scientific method is clearly represented and correctly explained.
Cards are detailed, colorful, and thoughtfully designed with creativity and precision.
Clear and confident explanation of the steps in your own words; video shows effort and understanding.

rubrics.title: Speed Racers: The Graphing Grand Prix

ratings.long_description: Correct use of Speed = Distance ÷ Time for each motion type
Results correctly match graph line types (constant, stopped, faster, slower, returning)
Work is organized, labeled, and photos are clear

rubrics.title: Engineered for Stability: The Skyscraper Challenge

ratings.long_description: Student submits a clear 3–5 sentence explanation describing gravity, wind, and support forces and how these forces affected their skyscraper. Shows accurate understanding of SC.6.P.13.1. (If there is no text box, leave your paragraph as a comment.)
Skyscraper is stable, reinforced, thoughtfully designed, and clearly shown in the submitted image. Structure meets height expectations (6–8 floors) and demonstrates engineering principles.

rubrics.title: Science Fair Mini-Experiments: Final Video Presentation

ratings.long_description: Clearly explains the scientific question, hypothesis, variables, and results using correct terminology. Demonstrates a strong understanding of the experiment and the science behind it.
Includes every required part from the Video Checklist (question, variables, results, claim, and reasoning). Follows directions fully.
Accurately presents data and uses it to support the claim. Reasoning connects evidence to the conclusion clearly and logically.
Demonstrates originality and enthusiasm. Uses visuals, posters, experiment clips, or creative editing to enhance the presentation.
Speaks clearly and confidently. Video is neat, organized, and well-planned. Shows strong effort and attention to detail.

rubrics.title: The Snowman Showdown: Mass vs. Gravity

ratings.long_description: Student submits a clear 3–5 sentence paragraph describing how mass affects gravitational pull and compares the large and small snowmen. Shows accurate understanding of SC.6.P.13.2.
Image shows both snowmen clearly, includes required decorations, sticky note labels, and demonstrates correct completion of the VR build.

rubrics.title: Candy Coated Forces: The Great Gingerbread Challenge

ratings.long_description: Student submits a clear 3–5 sentence paragraph describing their own experience with gravity, friction, and applied forces, and how these unbalanced forces changed motion in the gingerbread structure. Shows accurate understanding of SC.6.P.13.3.
Group gingerbread house is fully decorated, clearly visible, and demonstrates creativity, teamwork, and correct physics application.

rubrics.title: Science Fair Showcase: Scholar Review Panel

ratings.long_description: Answers are clear, thoughtful, encouraging, and reference specific videos or observations.
Student confirms watching at least 3 videos and describes at least two.
Student uploads a clear photo of their handwritten reflection page.

assignments.title: Saving Grace and Grades
assignments.html: This assignment is for failing scholars. No action is required on your part.

questions.text: Which statement best describes the Law of Conservation of Energy?

answers.text: Energy only exists as heat and light.
Energy can change forms but cannot be created or destroyed.
Energy can be destroyed when objects stop moving.
Energy can be created by machines but not destroyed.

questions.text: Friction always acts in the same direction as motion.
Which force pulls objects toward Earth and gives them weight?
Potential energy is energy of motion, while kinetic energy is stored energy.
When a roller coaster climbs up a hill and then rushes down the hill, what is the energy transformation that is happening?
Normal force acts upward from a surface to support the weight of an object.
A soccer ball begins to roll after being kicked. Which force caused the motion?
Energy can disappear completely if it changes into heat or sound.
Which situation shows balanced forces?

answers.text: A ball falling through the air
A book resting on a desk
A car speeding up on a hill

questions.text: Gravity is a contact force because objects must touch for it to act.
What is the first step of the scientific method?
Which formula is used to calculate speed?
The hypothesis is a random guess about what will happen in an experiment.
On a distance–time graph, what does a flat line mean?

answers.text: The object is moving at a constant speed

questions.text: During which step do scientists collect measurements, record data, and test their hypothesis?
A steeper line on a distance–time graph means the object is moving slower.
What do scientists do after they analyze their data?

answers.text: Draw a conclusion and share results
Ask new questions only if the experiment fails

questions.text: A runner travels 200 meters in 40 seconds. What is their speed?
Scientists sometimes repeat their experiments to check their results or improve accuracy.
Which statement about motion is correct?

answers.text: Motion happens when something changes position over time.
Motion only happens if an object is moving in a straight line.
Motion can only be measured in hours and miles.
Motion cannot be shown on a graph.

questions.text: The independent variable is the factor you measure during an experiment.
Which one is a dependent variable?
Controlled variables help make an experiment fair.
Which step comes first in the scientific method?
A hypothesis should be testable and based on research.
What type of energy does a moving object have?
Energy can be created if enough force is applied.
A stretched rubber band has what kind of energy?
A car travels 60 meters in 3 seconds. What is its speed?
A steeper line on a distance–time graph means faster motion.
Which force resists motion?
Gravity acts at a distance and does not require objects to touch.
Normal force pushes:
What causes gravity to be stronger?
Gravity becomes weaker as objects move farther apart.
When forces on an object are balanced, the object:
Unbalanced forces can change an object’s speed, direction, or both.
A soccer ball starts rolling because:

answers.text: An applied force acted on it

questions.text: What does a flat (horizontal) line on a distance–time graph show?

A student wonders whether hot or cold water dissolves sugar faster.

Which step comes next?
When a roller coaster goes down a hill, potential energy transforms into kinetic energy.
What happens to gravitational force when mass increases?
Speed is calculated by dividing time by weight.
A ball rolling across the floor slows down and stops mainly because of:
Gravity only pulls downward on Earth and does not exist in space.
